rv.q: Beetlejuice is frightfully addicting. You'll want to go again. Again. Again.

David Korins' set is ghoulishly fantastical and works hand-in-glove with Peter Nigrini's projections and Kenneth Posner's dazzling light design.

Beetlejuice's dramaturgy feels remarkably tight. The jokes remain genuinely funny despite its 2018 release, the macabre humor never tips into cruelty, and every delightfully strange character is afforded a satisfying, often surprising conclusion.
Fans of the film will enjoy the nostalgia and appreciate how naturally its theatricality translates to the stage, while newcomers can surrender to this very specific world.

The book by Scott Brown and Anthony King is hard to follow as narrative strands are thrown together in the most disorienting manner; it is hard to care about any of the characters' plights or contextual background.
"Beetlejuice" at Theatre takes the classic film and somehow breathes new life into it, even the dead characters.
Every aspect of the show, special effects, scenery, costumes, choreography, orchestra, is top-notch.
Ryan Stajmiger's Beetlejuice is everything this character should be. Hilarious, menacing, maniacal and, above all, entertaining.
His delivery was sharp and fearless, leaning fully into the character's chaotic charm.
There are subtleties I enjoyed through the musical.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this macabre carnival, praising its ghoulishly imaginative visuals and sharp humor, though some find the narrative disjointed. The production's over-the-top energy and technical spectacle win over most reviewers.
